headline: Employment Leave Bill Advances as Jobseeker Support Reaches 223,500
summary: Parliament advanced a contentious overhaul of employment leave rules while MPs clashed over rising jobseeker numbers and the effect of the economy on households. The House also passed legislation to improve public access to laws, began considering a Treaty settlement for Ngāti Ruapani mai Waikaremoana, and debated changes to public finance reporting before adjourning with that debate unfinished.

topicSummaries.topic: Employment Leave Bill Passes First Reading Amid Workers’ Rights Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed replacement for the Holidays Act would change how annual and sick leave are earned and paid, with potentially different effects for part-time and casual workers.
topicSummaries.content: Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden said the Employment Leave Bill would replace the complex Holidays Act with an hours-based system, provide leave from the first day of employment, and reduce payroll errors and compliance costs. It would give casual workers a 12.5 percent payment instead of leave accrual, while sick leave for part-time employees would be proportionate to their standard hours. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued that some workers could lose protections or entitlements and raised concerns about casualisation and limited worker consultation. National, ACT and New Zealand First supported the bill, which passed its first reading 68 votes to 55 and was referred to the Education and Workforce Committee for a report by 13 July.

keyExchanges.speaker: Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill introduces an hours-based accrual system for both annual leave and sick leave.

keyExchanges.speaker: Jan Tinetti (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The removal of holiday rights or entitlements from so-called casual workers and the way that that’s been translated, as it is written in this bill, and the replacement with an allowance removes a whole lot of rights from those particular workers.

topicSummaries.topic: Jobseeker Support Reaches 223,500 as Parties Dispute Economic Outlook
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The rising number of people receiving jobseeker support reflects pressure on workers and families and puts the Government’s employment targets under scrutiny.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Carmel Sepuloni pressed Social Development Minister Louise Upston on jobseeker numbers, youth unemployment and the Government’s reduction target. Upston said about 190,000 people were receiving the benefit when the Government took office and the December quarterly figure was 223,500; she attributed the increase to difficult economic conditions and argued that rising business confidence would support hiring. Sepuloni cited a record share of working-age people on the benefit, a 32 percent rise among 18- to 24-year-olds and a 10-year unemployment high. Upston acknowledged unemployment was higher than desired and said the Government was using case management and other welfare measures to help people into work.

keyExchanges.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is it a sign of green shoots when unemployment is at a 10-year high?

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: As of December, the quarterly figures show 223,500 people on jobseeker support, which is why our Government is focused on a more active welfare system to support people into work as conditions improve.

topicSummaries.topic: Public Finance Bill Debate Centres on Removal of Wellbeing Reporting
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes would alter what governments are required to report when explaining fiscal decisions, including whether they must account for wellbeing outcomes.
topicSummaries.content: The Public Finance Amendment Bill reached its third-reading debate, but the House adjourned before a vote, leaving the bill’s outcome unresolved. The Government said the bill would improve fiscal transparency, require a tax expenditure statement alongside the Budget and move the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update five working days earlier. It also removes the Act’s wellbeing requirements and allows alternative fiscal indicators. Labour’s Deborah Russell argued that removing mandatory wellbeing reporting would weaken scrutiny of social effects; the Government said the changes refocus the Act on public finance. The debate is due to resume at the next sitting.

keyExchanges.speaker: Scott Simpson (National)
keyExchanges.quote: These changes restore flexibility and ensure the focus of the Public Finance Act is on public finance.

keyExchanges.speaker: Deborah Russell (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The real problem we have with this bill, the real reason as to why we are so deeply opposed to it, is because it removes wellbeing budgeting from what the Government is required to report on.

topicSummaries.topic: Health Minister Details COVID Vaccine Advice to Ministers
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The exchange concerns what decision-makers were told about vaccine mandates for teenagers and how health advice should be disclosed and assessed.
topicSummaries.content: NZ First leader Winston Peters questioned Health Minister Simeon Brown about the COVID-19 Royal Commission’s findings on advice concerning two-dose vaccine mandates for 12- to 17-year-olds. Brown said the commission found that Chris Hipkins received a briefing on 22 December 2021 and that Ayesha Verrall considered it on 7 January 2022; he quoted advice suggesting younger people with one dose be permitted to work or undertake activities covered by mandates. Asked why the briefing had not been published, Brown said he did not know and referred the question to the Ministry of Health or Hipkins. Brown also said he had asked the Director-General of Health to ensure advice was clear to ministers and the public. Earlier in the sitting, he corrected a previous answer, saying the mandates remained in place until 4 April 2022, not late January.

keyExchanges.speaker: Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: Did the inquiry find that Ministers were informed of the concerns of the technical advisory group regarding risks to young people from double doses of vaccines; if so, what did the advice to Ministers say?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The briefing stated in paragraph 23, “In November 2021, CV TAG has raised concerns about vaccine mandates requiring younger age groups (e.g. [those under] 18 years) to be fully vaccinated. Consideration should be given to permitting younger people who have had one dose to be permitted to work or undertake other activities covered by the mandate.”

topicSummaries.topic: Opposition Challenges Government on Cook Strait Ferry Resilience
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Ferry disruptions can affect passengers and the movement of freight between the North and South Islands, while a replacement service remains years away.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Julie Anne Genter asked whether cancelling the previous ferry project would leave passengers and freight exposed to continuing disruption after another mechanical fault affected one of the two remaining Interislander ferries. Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour, answering for the Prime Minister, rejected the criticism, saying the previous proposal was unaffordable and unviable and pointing to a future pathway for rail-enabled ferries. Genter sought details of immediate steps to improve resilience before replacements arrive, but Seymour’s response focused on the longer-term plan and the Speaker ruled that he had addressed the question. No specific immediate measure was announced in the exchange.

keyExchanges.speaker: Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: What action, if any, will his Government take to increase the resilience of the ability of freight and people to cross the Cook Strait, given it’s three more years before we are going to get a replacement ferry?

keyExchanges.speaker: David Seymour (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government has created an affordable pathway to have rail-enabled ferries, with places that they can be loaded and unloaded at either end, that are actually viable and affordable.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Defends Shift to Administrative Data for Census
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Census data informs public funding, electoral boundaries and representation, so any undercount could affect communities’ visibility in public decisions.
topicSummaries.content: Te Pāti Māori MP Tākuta Ferris questioned a proposed move away from a traditional five-yearly census towards using administrative data, smaller surveys and targeted collection, citing concerns from Te Kāhui Raraunga that the approach could undercount Māori. Statistics Minister Shane Reti said the current model was financially and operationally unsustainable and argued that integrated administrative data could improve population counts. He acknowledged the concerns and committed Stats New Zealand to working with iwi Māori and Te Kāhui Raraunga on the approach, but did not offer a guarantee against undercounting.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tākuta Ferris (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he agree with analysis from Te Kāhui Raraunga that replacing the five-yearly census with administrative data, small-sample surveys, and targeted data collection “will build in a bias that favours numerically dominant groups, and will further invisibilise some Māori individuals, whānau, and communities”?

keyExchanges.speaker: Shane Reti (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Stats New Zealand is confident in the use of integrated administrative data at counting the population even better than a full-field enumeration census.

topicSummaries.topic: $24 Million Ngāti Ruapani Settlement Bill Advances to Committee
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The settlement provides financial redress and land-related measures intended to support Ngāti Ruapani’s cultural, economic and intergenerational connections to its rohe.
topicSummaries.content: Parliament gave the Ngāti Ruapani mai Waikaremoana Claims Settlement Bill its first reading and referred it to the Māori Affairs Committee, with a report due by 27 July. Treaty Negotiations Minister Paul Goldsmith said the Crown apology addresses historical breaches, including land loss and the treatment of Lake Waikaremoana. The package includes $24 million in financial and commercial redress, two cultural redress properties totalling 50 hectares, restoration of about 12,000 hectares into Te Urewera and the return of traditional names to six places. MPs from across parties expressed support for progressing the bill, while Willie Jackson noted that the settlement could not fully compensate for losses and Oriini Kaipara stressed the importance of iwi authority and the Crown honouring its commitments.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: However, I believe this settlement lays a cultural and economic foundation for Ngāti Ruapani to strengthen their connection to their rohe and to grow their identity for future generations to come.

keyExchanges.speaker: Willie Jackson (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: $24 million’s not going to get them interested; it’s not enough, but it’s a start.

topicSummaries.topic: Legislation Amendment Bill Passes With Green Party Opposition
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The law will make it easier for the public to find secondary legislation, while changing how some technical updates to legislation may be made.
topicSummaries.content: The Legislation Amendment Bill passed its third reading by 108 votes to 15, with the Green Party opposing it. It requires agencies to publish secondary legislation consistently and keep it up to date, with the New Zealand Legislation website intended to become a central access point. Labour and other supporters backed the accessibility changes but raised questions about safeguards, including the expanded scope for revision bills, which can update legislation through a streamlined process. The Greens said that scope could allow changes that are more than minor without sufficient parliamentary scrutiny. The Government said safeguards would remain, and Labour supported the bill while calling for the new system to be monitored.

keyExchanges.speaker: James Meager (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The purpose of this bill is straightforward. It is to make legislation easier to find, to use, and to understand.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lawrence Xu-Nan (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: We are concerned that the expanded scope of revision bills under clause 37 would mean that it is much easier for any Government to push through amendments that are not minor in nature but that may, potentially, substantially change the nature or the purpose of a bill

conclusion: The sitting produced concrete legislative progress, but the central political divide remained whether proposed reforms will ease pressure on households and employers or weaken protections and accountability.
